title: ASASSN-14ko optical half-rises tied to the X-ray dip show a shorter period again after 2023 and slow flare rises only while the period was constant; flare 41 forecast for 2026 November 10-15
abstract: Question: the soft X-ray dips of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko repeat at a constant 108.44 d in 2020-2024, but the 2024-2026 optical flares seemed early, and flare shapes changed after 2021. Is the early arrival real, and which clock survives? Approach: we fitted all ASAS-SN g flares of 2017-2025 and the TESS rises of flares 14 and 38 (MCMC), measured the lag of each optical and UV marker on the X-ray deep-suppression dip of the same cycle (seven cycles), built a dip-referenced timing set with fixed sampling and shape rules, and compared clock models and frozen published clocks. Results: the optical half-rise follows the dip by 4.75 +/- 0.52 d with no excess scatter (chi2 1.6 for 5 dof), as stable as the UVW2 peak; optical peaks and two-component markers are not stable. Broad 2022-2023 flares (rise sigma 7-13 d, with optical precursors) give early half-rises and late UV peaks and are removed. The narrow flares 34 (ASAS-SN) and 38 (TESS) remain 3.1 +/- 0.6 and 7.5 +/- 0.7 d early relative to the constant X-ray clock; a constant period is worse by Delta AIC 17-32 (5-8 without flare 38). On cycles 12-38 the best clocks decrease at -0.53 +/- 0.04 d per cycle until cycle 21, keep 108.43 d, then change by a step of -1.23 +/- 0.20 d after cycle 32 or by a ramp of -0.17 +/- 0.03 d per cycle (Delta AIC 0.7). The frozen two-break clock is rejected (Delta AIC 10-26); the frozen precessing star-disc drag clock fits (Delta AIC 0-7.6). Flare rises were broader in the constant-clock era (median sigma 7.1 against 2.9 d; Mann-Whitney p = 0.012-0.036). Forecast: dip of flare 41 on 2026 November 6-10, optical half-rise November 10-15 (constant clock: November 26). Limitations: six calibration cycles; the post-2024 result rests on two narrow flares and one SPHEREx peak; the shape cut was set after inspection at the edge of the calibration range; step and ramp are not separable.

Right: 2024-2027 and forecasts.
Lag of optical and UV markers on the X-ray deep-suppression dip of the same cycle, and the reduced chi-square of a constant lag. The optical half-rise and the UVW2 peak keep a constant lag.

citations.reason: We use its UVW2 peak times and its constant X-ray clock. We confirm its early 2024-2026 markers with shape control and a dip-referenced lag.
Its f30 deep-suppression dip times are our reference clock and lag calibration; its X-ray visit rates give the pre-dip X-ray level.
We use its ASAS-SN Sky Patrol, TESS and Swift UVOT light curves.
We score its frozen clock curves: the precessing drag clock M3 fits our independent timing set; its two-break clock M2 is rejected.
We use its SPHEREx peak time of flare 37.
It found slower rises after 2021; we show that slow rises occurred only in the constant-clock era and returned to narrow rises after 2024.
We use its mass-loss kick energy scale for the step estimate.
